extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians and theoretical physicists interested in the interaction between mathematics and physics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological principles for assessing and assimilating physical models and methods into mathematics (e.g., mean-field models, asymptotic reasoning, and heuristic physicists' methods). Focuses on when models count as good explanations, the role of rigour, and strategies for mathematical uptake of physical ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative adequacy of models
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical models should exhibit some of the key qualitative features of the physical system they are intended to depict (e.g., the Curie–Weiss mean-field model exhibits a phase transition and spontaneous magnetization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Weiss's self-consistent equation η = tanh(η/T) shows a phase transition even though numerical predictions disagree with measurements. Such qualitative resemblance is taken as evidence that 'we are mathematically on the right track' and justifies using the model as a starting point in investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability despite numerical inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A model may be valuable even if its numerical values are not in accord with physical measurements; qualitative agreement can suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mean-field theory is the usual starting point for workers in statistical mechanics investigating a new system despite well-known shortcomings; usefulness derives from capturing broad features rather than precise numerics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical well-definedness and rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical methods and objects ought to be well defined and treated with rigour; physicists' methods often fall short of this mathematical standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers/mathematicians require well-defined quantities and objects to adapt physical ideas reliably. The text warns that physicists' informal methods can leave the 'objects themselves' not mathematically well defined, creating obstacles for mathematical assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferential restrictions (physicists' rules of thumb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners (physicists) manage lack of rigour by restricting which inferences are drawn from questionable methods, using rules of thumb to avoid error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kevin Davey's analysis: examples like the Dirac delta and Feynman path integrals illustrate that physicists tolerate non-rigorous reasoning because they limit its use; however, the boundary between secure and questionable inferences is often unclear, posing problems for formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of asymptotic methods / asymptotic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific models often employ asymptotic methods that 'eliminate both detail, and, in some sense, precision', and rely on asymptotic reasoning to explain emergent properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Batterman's account: such methods are pervasive (e.g., in critical phenomena) and have implications for explanation, reduction, and emergence; evaluators should note when a model's justification depends on asymptotic limits rather than finite-detail fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two assimilation strategies for physical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two broad strategies for incorporating physicists' ideas into mathematics: (1) treat the ideas as heuristic and then prove the resulting conjectures by conventional mathematical means; (2) rework and formalize the physicists' ideas to create new conceptual schemes that validate some of their calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first is conservative (heuristic → conventional proof); the second is more radical (retooling physics concepts into new rigorous frameworks). Dyson and the chapter's author emphasize the second as productive in many historical cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek juxtaposition of incompatible concepts as opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify empirical situations where disparate or incompatible mathematical concepts are juxtaposed; these present opportunities to create broader conceptual frameworks that harmonize the pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dyson's methodological principle: look for unexplained juxtapositions and develop wider frameworks in which they coexist; historically fruitful for mathematicians engaging with physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinjection of empirical ideas to prevent degeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: When a mathematical subject becomes overly abstract or 'baroque' it risks degeneration; reinjecting empirical ideas revitalizes and preserves the subject's vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann's warning: returning to empirical sources can rejuvenate mathematics; evaluators should consider empirical connections as healthy checks on abstract development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish model types and their mathematical equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating mean-field or similar models, distinguish different mathematical categories (e.g., Weiss-type macroscopic mean vs Husimi/Kac interaction models where each microscopic variable interacts with many others); they are not necessarily equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two types of mean-field models can behave differently even for paradigmatic cases like Curie–Weiss; careful analysis is needed before treating one as a stand-in for the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criteria when empirical tests are absent
rubrics_metrics.description: In domains lacking direct empirical tests (e.g., string theory), practitioners may rely on aesthetic criteria (simplicity, beauty, coherence) analogous to those of pure mathematics to guide theory choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes that the absence of experimental access shifts emphasis to aesthetic/mathematical virtues; this affects how acceptance and convergence between mathematics and physics proceed and should be acknowledged when evaluating such theories.
